- Signatur: SZ-AAL/B1.133
- Datum: 1.6.1941
- Objekttyp: Brief

pages.transcription:
New York, June 1st, 1941
Dear Hanna & Manfred,
There was no letter from you last week and
also from our side there is little to report. We had a letter
from Eva that she is well and everything is fine, and next
Sunday I hope to be able to visit her again, and perhaps
Stefan will come with me. If Sunday were not his best and quietest
working day, he would accompany me more often, but as we had
so many little business things to settle which take lots of time
without bringing profit he hates to lose any more time. This
weekend we had to go to Atlantic City - the super-Brighton of USA -
to visit a lawyer-friend who advises us in our personal decisions
and our next plans. I wrote you that we had given up the return
to Brazil for the time being although life down there is much
cheaper, easier and quieter. And I am glad to remain near Eva
and to convince myself regularly how well she is settled in Boston
and how much she likes being there. From Salmon's none of us has
ever heard again since many weeks and we have decided to forget
about them. They are the type of people who only see what is
under their nose and who do not think. And fortunately we
do not need them. - Kiefer's have visited Eva a fortnight ago, we
are near - and will not leave New York before the end of July. -
Franz Newman as well as Berner's (Rose Wohl's brother-in-law) have
taken out their car again after the winter storage and promised
to visit her, and Elisabeth is only expecting the school holidays
in order to have Eva for a few days. From mother I have
not heard for a few weeks, and I attribute it to the fact that
she wrote by ordinary mail the last months. She must have
been very happy to see you both again. Stefan had two more
or less private letters from Eisen, and is somewhat disappointed
that his friend Ruben is not in his house as he expected after
earlier news. He fully understands the difficulties under which
he works, but he requests you not to give him any more help
until he has spent all his money he got for this purpose.
From my friend Lotte I heard that she was in the country
with the Raeburn family but that she intended to leave
them in June and to return to London. I suppose she will
then communicate with you at least by phone. - I wrote
you last time that we were trying to find out from through
Washington whether your brother's affidavit is sufficient
but we got no reply so far. Authorities here work very slowly, just
as the whole tempo here is not at all "American" as we imagined
it in Europe.

I do not think that you missed very much because you
could not hear those Penclub dinner speeches. For me it was
quite interesting and entertaining because it was my first
big public dinner, sitting at the celebrities' table between
Somerset Maugham (who was very nice at not at all stiff as I
imagined him to be) and Count Sforza. Most of the European
writers whom we ever read were present and I hope it was not
disappointing for the thousand people who paid 3 dollars each
for this privilege to see that writers really do not look
different from other people. There were lots of speeches, and
fortunately, on account of the radio, the speakers were strictly
rationed in time - Stefan, Jules Romains, Maugham, Dorothy Thompson,
Sigrid Undset between 6 and 10 minutes, the others who spoke in
their native languages to two minutes each. Then there was
the inevitable auction to raise money for refugee funds and
we were surprised that really a number of people publicly
donated three and four hundred dollars each. They raised about
5000 dollars and that will be just sufficient to pay the
travelling expenses of 10 persons from Europe as they can only
get out by the most phantastic routes - via Russia and Japan or
via Africa and Martinique and only a few lucky people via
Lisbon direct to USA. Unfortunately the possibilities for affi-
davits become more and more limited among the people we
know, and we have not yet succeeded in finding one for Friederike.
I wrote to Jan in this respect so you need not give him my
earlier letter at all. Should he come to you again for help
you might let him have ten or fifteen pounds and tell
him that with this the money you had at your disposition
is exhausted. - I hope you all keep well and that you
are definitely through with the dentist. By the way, you never
mention how your heart stands all the strain. Do tell me whether
it gives you any trouble. This is much more important to me
than my own health about which you seemed to worry quite
unnecessarily for I can do and really do everything that can
be done for it while you certainly neglect those things.
By the way mail is now much more regular and therefore
it is worth while, and we would be glad, that you always inform
us by cable a week or ten days before when you go to Bath. -
I hope you did not mind that our birthday telegram was sent collect.
I felt a little doubtful about doing so but Stefan said you
would understand. Kindest regards and best love and kisses
Lotte
